citation: Chicago Tribune, May 17, 1882, interview with Capt. Thomas S. Eells of Jacksonville, Fla., who landed at Chicago in 1832 with Gurdon S. Hubbard and came back for the Calumet Club's Old-Settlers' reunion.
locator: the interview at Secretary Hotchkiss's office of the Lumberman's Exchange, from “It seems to me … that I have awakened from a Rip Van Winkle sleep” to the razor-hone bequest signed “THOMAS S. EELLS… One of the old settlers of 1832”
rights_note: Chicago Tribune, 1882: a United States imprint long out of copyright.
access_notes: READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, NOT AT THE PAGE — see chicagology_goldenage_063. THE PAGE'S DATELINES FOR TWO OF THESE DOCUMENTS READ 1892 AND THE DOCUMENTS ARE OF 1882. The page heads the Eells interview "Chicago Tribune, May 17, 1892" and the reception report "Chicago Tribune, May 19, 1892", and prints Eells's own bequest over the date "May 18, 1892". Six things inside the text put all three in 1882: the Tribune of 25 April 1882 announces the FOURTH annual reception for 18 May and the report calls itself the fourth; Eells says "I came here fifty years ago" of 1832; he gives his birth as 1814 and his age as 68; he says the razor-hone left with him "in Chicago in 1833" has been kept "forty-nine years"; he calls Gurdon S. Hubbard, born 1802, "over 80 years of age" and dines with him the next day, which no 1892 interview could do; and the death roll he shares the page with is Wentworth's list of 1881-82. The dates carried in these records are therefore 1882, and the page's own datelines are recorded here rather than followed.
note: A RECOLLECTION OF 1832 GIVEN FIFTY YEARS LATER, and three years early for this scene. It is townscape evidence and it is worth what a fifty-year-old memory is worth: no building in this project is placed on it.
